22.14.4.en: Paradise of the Fathers * He who quibbles in the face of discipline drives away from himself the fatherly mercies. He who murmurs against trials has them multiplied upon him. He who is not disciplined here and crushed by trials is tormented there without mercy.

22.14.5.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * Rejoice that God visits you, and keep this blessed saying on your lips: “The Lord hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death” (Ps 118:18). Even if you are iron, the fire has burned the rust off you, and if you are righteous and fall ill, you will go from strength to strength. And remember what is written: “If so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together” (Rom 8:17).

22.14.6.en: St. Amma Syncletica * She was asked: “How should a person rebuke?” She said: “As a father rebukes his son, and as the physician’s purpose is to heal the sick.

22.14.7.en: * And she was also asked: “How should rebuke be received?” She said: “As a child receives the discipline of his father and the sick man the treatment of his physician.”

22.14.8.en: St. Basil the Great * Let us receive trials as we receive medicines from the physician so that we may be saved, and as we receive discipline from the father so that we may be trained. For this reason the wise man said: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare thy soul for temptation” (Sir 2:1).

22.14.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * Once again, after a long time, love compels me to strike you with the rod of Christ, which is for discipline and rebuke, so that the word of Scripture may be fulfilled in us: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Prov 27:6), and what follows. And again, if we discipline you, do not faint, but remember the saying: “My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Heb 12:5-6). But even if I rebuke you, you are not ignorant of the Apostle’s saying: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2 Tim 4:2).

22.15.0.en: St. Barsanuphius and his disciple John He that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches, and he that giveth to the rich, shall surely come to want [16].

22.15.1.en: The wise man condemns two practices carried out for the purpose of acquiring gain or increasing resources: oppressing the poor, and giving gifts or bribes to the rich for the sake of material advantage or to obtain honour and authority. Both are hateful, even if they achieve temporary success, for they remove the Lord’s blessing from the man, and he comes into spiritual and material want.

22.15.2.en: Many have become poor through their oppression of the poor or their generosity in giving to the rich, not out of love but to obtain vain glory!

22.16.s.en: 7. Resorting to the counsel of the wise

22.16.0.en: 17 Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge. 18 For it is a pleasant thing if thou keep them within thee; if they be fixed together upon thy lips. 19 That thy trust may be in the Lord, I have made known to thee this day, even to thee. 20 Have not I written to thee excellent things in counsels and knowledge, 21 That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth; that thou mightest answer the words of truth to them that send unto thee?

22.16.1.en: Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge [17].

22.16.2.en: Solomon felt the value of wisdom and went on at length in praising it, especially in the book of Wisdom (Wis 7-9), counting it better than the throne and the scepter (Wis 7:8), and than wealth (Wis 7:8), as well as than health and beauty, and even than visible light, for it is the source of sciences and knowledge, a reflection of the divine light (Wis 7:17 etc.), and he asked that it be the companion of his life (Wis 9). It is the bride who bestows glory, the immortal one, who sits on the heavenly throne. He wishes that the whole world might enjoy union with the wisdom of God.

22.16.3.en: * The monk ought to take counsel from a wise man, and not let the counsel of a fool dwell in his heart.

22.16.4.en: St. Hyperechius the Priest * Brother, the Holy Bible says: “Do all things with counsel” (Prov 24:6), and “Do nothing without counsel” (Sir 32:24). When you acted without counsel, but by your own will, you were not struggling with your mind. For there is none who does not need counsel except God alone, who created wisdom; but when you sought to cut off your passion according to God and to attain humility, and to take me, your very little brother, as a guide, you stirred up the envy of Satan, the enemy of good, who envies all people continually.

22.16.5.en: * Submit yourself to a teacher, that he may discipline you with mercy. “Do nothing without counsel” (Sir 32:19) even if things seem good to you, for the light of the demons finally becomes darkness. If you hear or think or see anything that leaves even a little disturbance in your heart, know that it is from the demons.

22.16.6.en: St. Barsanuphius * In Jerusalem there was a virgin who was shut in for six years, wearing sackcloth, and her asceticism was excessive, and she never ate anything pleasant. The Fathers forbade her this, but she did not listen to anyone’s counsel, and so she was stripped of God’s help because of her arrogance and self-admiration; the guardian of her chastity departed from her, and she fell a hideous fall. She brought in to her a man who used to serve her, and fell into sin with him. This calamity came upon her because she made the purpose of her asceticism to be show, and not for the love of God, and she thought herself better than many. When pomp took hold of her, she fell into the hand of the devil.

22.16.7.en: Paradise of the Fathers Everyone needs the counsel of a wise father of confession or a wise guide, even the solitary monk, however long his experience in the holy life and in fellowship with God. In the discourse of St. Gregory, head of the hermits of Cyprus, who departed at the end of the fourth century, he directs the attention of the hermits to the danger of a man relying on his own wisdom and not seeking the counsel of his father in a spirit of humility, for in this there is a hindrance to the practice of all the virtues and their uprooting, since the demons are given authority over him.

22.16.8.en: * Hear me, my brethren the monks, and guard this way of life, in which the salvation of your souls and their life is hidden and kept: Do not rely on your wisdom or on your knowledge, but follow in humility the counsel of your fathers, for doubt is a hindrance to all the virtues and uproots them, and is like a prison that binds all its disciples in ignorance, for they think that they will enter the Kingdom of Heaven without many afflictions.

22.16.9.en: * Because of their disobedience to the counsel of their spiritual fathers and their exhortation, the demons stripped them of the work of the holy virtues and filled them with all that Paul spoke of, for they thought that without the love of God and the keeping of His commandments they could attain and take for themselves the divine rest and the joy that is given to the hermits for their active labor.

22.17.0.en: St. Gregory, head of the hermits of Cyprus For it is a pleasant thing if thou keep them within thee; if they be fixed together upon thy lips [18].

22.17.1.en: He asks the hearer to treasure wisdom in his heart, and as we said before, the “heart” among the Jews is equivalent to the “mind” among the Greeks, and both mean the inner man.

22.17.2.en: Wisdom is kept in the heart and fixed upon the lips, so that the person has no other speech than what proceeds from the inner wisdom.

22.18.0.en: That thy trust may be in the Lord, I have made known to thee this day, even to thee [19].

22.18.1.en: No one enjoys true wisdom without relying on the Giver of wisdom.

22.19.0.en: Have not I written to thee excellent things in counsels and knowledge [20].

22.19.1.en: The wise man affirms that what he writes is not mere human wisdom, nor the fruit of human experience alone, but that he writes excellent things concerning our fellowship with God.

22.19.2.en: The literal translation of the Hebrew text is: “Have I not set it before you in three ways” or “a third time.” The text in the Septuagint is: “You describe the matters to yourself in three ways according to the breadth of your heart.”

22.19.3.en: * He who opens his heart with purity contemplates the words of God in their practical, physical and theological meanings. Therefore the whole body of Scripture can be divided into three parts: ethical, physical and theological. The book of Proverbs corresponds to the first part, Ecclesiastes to the second, and the Song of Songs to the third.

22.19.4.en: St. Evagrius * Just as human beings consist of body, soul and spirit, so the Holy Bible consists of the body of the letters, from which the ignorant person benefits, and which is called “the manual teaching.” The second consists of the soul, which is a higher meaning, understood by one who is more learned. And it also contains a spirit, which is the highest and the most spiritual contemplation, which the perfect speak and understand.

22.20.0.en: St. John Chrysostom That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth; that thou mightest answer the words of truth to them that send unto thee? [21].

22.20.1.en: If the wise man in his love offers the light of divine truth and wisdom to the one who asked him, he requires the asker in turn to offer it to the one who sent him. Wisdom is offered to every person, to Solomon himself, to the one who came as a messenger to ask him, and to the one who sent this messenger.

22.20.2.en: Wisdom is a deposit of love; keeping it does not lie in hiding it, but in a man’s longing that all his brethren may enjoy it, offering it faithfully.

22.21.0.en: 22 Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate: 23 For the Lord will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them.

22.21.1.en: Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate [22].

22.21.2.en: Cases were heard at the gate of the city, and perhaps the choice of the courts of justice at the gates of the city carries a symbol that no unjust man, usurper or evildoer may enter the city. Here he gives a warning to the ruler and the judge and those who share with them in the courts of justice, against those who rob the poor man of his right and wrong him for the sake of the rich or those in authority.

22.22.0.en: For the Lord will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them [23].

22.22.1.en: There is the Judge of judges and King of kings who specializes in defending the wronged, especially the poor and needy, who have none to inquire after them. He pleads their cause against the unjust judges, and judges the unjust with what they judged unjustly against others, so He spoils the spoilers. It is as though he who robs the needy man and presses upon him is robbing himself and pressing upon his own depths, as it is said in Obadiah: “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head” (Obad 15).

22.22.2.en: * “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee” (Obad 15). Such is the order of nature, that each one receives the same treatment with which he treats others, and the recompense is returned to him exactly equal to the deeds he practices.

22.23.s.en: 9. Keeping company with an angry man

22.23.0.en: 24 Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: 25 Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.

22.23.1.en: Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go [24].

22.23.2.en: The wise man looks upon anger and wrath as a dangerous plague whose infection can spread quickly, so he warns us not to be in the company of an angry man, or even to walk with a furious man on the road. “Evil communications corrupt good manners” (1 Cor 15:33).

22.23.3.en: * To live among those who are without conscience and who are deceivers in their regard for keeping the commandments is dangerous, as is clear from Solomon’s following words: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not walk, lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.

22.24.0.en: St. Basil the Great Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul [25].

22.24.1.en: Let a man not rely on himself, thinking that friendship with an angry man and walking with a furious man cannot affect his conduct, for being lenient with oneself and accepting fellowship with the furious is a snare that a man sets for himself.

22.25.s.en: 10. Wisdom in going surety for others

22.25.0.en: Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts [26].

22.26.0.en: If thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? [27].

22.26.1.en: Here he returns to repeat in the book his warning against being careless in going surety for the debts of a person or of reckless people, for because of this surety a man may lose even his bed on which he sleeps. We were warned before in Proverbs 6:1 and 17:18, and I have already commented on this warning.

22.26.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) used this warning while writing on pastoral care: it is fitting for superiors and leaders to care for the salvation of those under their leadership, lest their blood be required of them, as being sureties for them or responsible for them.

22.26.3.en: * We must therefore offer exhortation to subordinates, lest they receive a severer punishment if they are not justified even in their personal capacity; as for superiors, let them beware lest they be judged because of the faults of their subordinates, even if they are indifferent to their own deeds.

22.26.4.en: We must exhort the flock to care for itself, for the greater this care, the less it is entangled in caring for others. Likewise we must exhort the others (the shepherds) to fulfil their responsibility for the flock with wisdom, without neglecting their responsibility for themselves.

22.26.5.en: Scripture says to those who are slothful in caring for their own affairs: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Prov 6:6). But to the other comes the fearful warning in the words of Scripture: “My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, thou art snared with the words of thy mouth, thou art taken with the words of thy mouth” (Prov 6:1-2). It is clear that he who goes surety for his friend takes upon himself the responsibility for the soul of another person by guaranteeing his conduct, and if he strikes his hand with a stranger, the mind is occupied with a new responsibility, and likewise when he is snared with the words of his mouth, and taken with the words in him, for if he speaks good words about those for whom he is responsible, he must needs watch over the subject of his speech. The speech is snared in his mouth because there is an urgent necessity that he rein himself in with prudence, lest negligence and slackness creep into his life, which would not agree with his teaching. Accordingly Scripture adds to the previous words the good exhortation: “Do this now, my son, and deliver thyself, when thou art come into the hand of thy friend; go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend. Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids” (Prov 6:3-4). For the shepherd who has taken the responsibility of others upon himself, as an example by his life, must be on guard not only for himself but must labor to raise up the brethren of his flock.

22.27.0.en: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set [28].

22.27.1.en: This can be understood as an affirmation of the commandment given by Moses the prophet (Deut 19:14), where he required every tribe, when receiving its portion in the land of promise, not to remove the landmarks of its boundaries and so seize from the fields or lands of the surrounding tribes. It is a commandment to every believer to be faithful in his dealings, not to cheat in the scales, and not to seize the right of his neighbor or relative. It can also be interpreted spiritually, as we saw before, namely that we keep the deposit of the faith, that is, the Tradition concerning the doctrines of the faith, without change.

22.27.2.en: Origen and other Fathers see in this commandment that what we received from the early Church concerning the canonical books of the Holy Bible and the Creed are the ancient landmarks set by our fathers under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, which we must preserve.

22.27.3.en: * We do not allow the faith or the Creed, defined by our holy fathers assembled in the days of the Council of Nicaea, to be shaken by anyone, nor do we entrust ourselves or others to replace a word of what they set down, or to tamper with a letter of it. For we remember him who said: “Remove not the landmark which thy fathers have set.”

22.27.4.en: St. Cyril the Great Some see that moving the landmark is to transgress the limits of the virtues, so that they turn into vices.

22.27.5.en: * He who moves the boundary of godliness turns it into superstitious beliefs or into evil. And he who moves the boundary of courage changes it into recklessness or cowardice. In the same way this applies to the other virtues as well as to doctrines and other matters of the faith.

22.27.6.en: This also concerns the teaching about the Holy Trinity. For whoever denies the divinity of the Holy Spirit denies Baptism, and whoever calls others gods brings in a whole temple of pagan gods.

22.28.0.en: Seest thou a man diligent in his business?

22.28.2.en: he shall not stand before mean men! [29]

22.28.3.en: A renewed and repeated call to a life of striving and faithfulness in family life, work and worship, so that we may hear the divine voice: “Thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.” The diligent man stands with boldness before the King of kings, to enjoy the divine embrace, but the slothful man’s portion is with the mean, that is, the unfaithful demons.

22.28.4.en: * Cursed is he who hides the wheat at the time of sowing (see Prov 11:26), for the divine parable [of the talents (Mt 25:14-30)] requires us not to neglect the gift or hide it without increasing and multiplying it, or else we shall justly be cast out as wicked murmurers. On this basis the Lord praised those who multiplied their talents, saying: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord (Mt 25:23).

22.28.5.en: * There is a commandment from the Apostle to his disciple that obliges him not to let the grace given to us be idle and without profit. And he affirms, saying to him, not to neglect the gift given to him. For he that tilleth his land is satisfied with bread, but the way of the slothful man is full of thorns. And the Spirit warns us not to fall into this (sloth), saying: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” (Jer 4:3). And the prophet shows the end of such sloth, saying: “Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer 10:48). For the servant of God must be diligent and careful. Yes, rather he must be fervent as fire, so that when he crushes the fleshly lusts with a fervent spirit he may be able to draw near to God, whom the saints call “a consuming fire.”

22.28.7.en: For my sake You became poor, that You might make me rich!

22.28.8.en: * Let me possess You, who for my sake became poor; in You I become rich, so my soul lacks nothing, for You are my virtue and my wealth!

22.28.9.en: * In You I look upon all humanity, and I see all as the work of Your hands; all are born naked, and go out of the world naked; You are the glory and honour of man!

22.28.10.en: * The storms of evil blow, and I take refuge in You, O Rock of ages.

22.28.11.en: I clothe myself with Your humility, and You pour Your splendor upon me.

22.28.12.en: You keep me from the thorns of the world and the snares of the enemy.

22.28.13.en: * In the waters of Baptism I put on the garment of sonship; I became a child ascribed to You.

22.28.14.en: Let me receive all discipline and training from Your hands,

22.28.15.en: so that I may grow and enjoy true maturity.

22.28.16.en: * I flee from strife and contention, and let malice have no place in my heart.

22.28.17.en: You grant me peace and purity of heart; You give grace to my lips, so that they overflow with the honey of Your love.

22.28.18.en: You open my inner sight, and pour into me the knowledge of love.

22.28.19.en: * In You I go out to work with all diligence, for You are always working for my sake.

22.28.20.en: No enticement draws me, as long as You fill all my depths!

22.28.21.en: * I will not close my hand to the poor, nor wrong a hired servant, nor bribe a rich man for material benefit or to obtain honour!

22.28.22.en: * Let me possess Your humility, and so submit to the counsel of the wise,

22.28.23.en: and not rely in pride on my own opinion!

22.28.24.en: * My depths cry out to Your wisdom:

22.28.26.en: And my lips are silent, so as to speak only according to your counsel.

22.28.27.en: * Grant me Your tenderness, that I may be merciful to all.

22.28.28.en: Let me not mock a poor man or rob him of his right, nor despise a needy man and wrong him.

22.28.29.en: For You are the Father of all, the Judge of the wronged, and the defender of those who have none to inquire after them.

22.28.30.en: * In my companionship with You, I do not walk with an angry man in his way, nor do I find rest with a murmuring, furious man.

22.28.31.en: I will not accept walking on a road in which You are not.

22.28.32.en: And I will lean on no one but Your breast!

22.28.33.en: * You grant me Your wisdom, so I bear the spirit of discernment, and do not confuse virtue with vice!

22.28.34.en: Nor do I mix light with darkness.

22.28.35.en: * Who gives me the spirit of faithfulness but You? Who supports me in my striving but You?

22.28.36.en: In You I am faithful in everything!
